title: Bridgetown summit asks countries to agree an AI risk framework within a year
excerpt: A UN and Barbados summit on AI safety closed with a call for a multilateral AI risk framework with independent oversight, plus testing, incident reporting and kill switches in public purchasing.

sources.title: Bridgetown Special Summit on AI Safety: Bridgetown Call to Action on AI Safety for Humanity
Government of Barbados and United Nations: press release, Bridgetown Special Summit closes with Call to Action (PDF)
UN News: Bridgetown AI summit to tackle safety as risks outpace capacity to respond
Al Jazeera: UN chief calls for world to agree on AI oversight within a year

body_html:
A one-day summit on AI safety in Bridgetown, the capital of Barbados, ended on 23 November 2026 with a call for governments to agree, within the next year, a shared international framework for managing AI risks. The meeting was co-hosted by the Government of Barbados and the United Nations, with Prime Minister Mia Amor Mottley and UN Secretary-General António Guterres.

The closing document, the Bridgetown Call to Action on AI Safety for Humanity, asks UN member states to develop "a globally inclusive and principles-based Multilateral Framework for AI risk management, backed by independent and credible oversight." It is not a treaty and creates no legal duties. Ahead of the summit, a UN official described the proposal to UN News as a framework countries can use to build their own national AI safety arrangements, not as regulation.

What the Call to Action asks for

The document groups its appeals under three headings. On safety and risk management, it calls for:

  • international cooperation on accountability, liability, insurance and enforcement when AI causes harm;
  • shared baselines for transparency and accountability by those who build and those who deploy AI;
  • testing before and after release, and independent evaluation, including in local languages;
  • international incident reporting, notification and response, for both routine problems and emergencies.

On capacity, it asks governments to build safety into the AI they buy, including requiring kill switches from the moment of purchase, and to strengthen institutions that manage and respond to AI risks, particularly in the Global South. It also states plainly that humans must control AI, and not the other way round.

The organisers' press release says the summit had over 250 participants from governments, technology companies, AI safety institutes, science and civil society, and points to a proposed Global Fund for AI Capacity-Building that aims to raise about US$3 billion in initial commitments. In it, Mr Guterres says safety must come first as the technology spreads, and that every country must be included.

Why a small country hosted it

Many countries have no means to test AI systems or respond when something goes wrong. Before the meeting, UN News cited a large gap between richer and poorer countries in the number of teams that handle cyber incidents. The Call to Action's focus on testing in local languages and on shared regional capacity reflects that gap. In the press release, Ms Mottley said a country "cannot protect its people from systems it has no means to understand or oversee."

What is still unknown

The published pages do not list which countries or organisations have endorsed the Call, and no country has committed to a specific framework text. Al Jazeera notes that international agreement looks difficult while major AI powers compete. The Call names follow-up venues, including the Geneva AI Summit and the UN process, and mentions plans for new institutional arrangements in the next 6 to 18 months.

Why it matters for staying in charge

Several of the Call's appeals match the Humasure Directives. A kill switch from the point of purchase is a practical form of D1, Always stoppable. Independent evaluation and clear liability reflect D9, Accountable. Incident reporting across a product's life links to D10, Safe for its whole life. The common thread is that people in every country, not only the largest ones, should be able to check AI systems and stop them when needed.
